data.title: Why Belite Bio shares are falling today
data.description:
What happened?

Shares of Belite Bio fell 14.5% in the afternoon session after the company announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) extended the review period for the New Drug Application (NDA) for tinlarebant for the treatment of Stargardt disease type 1 by three months.

The three-month review extension may have weighed on shares by delaying the decision on tinlarebant and prolonging uncertainty for investors. Under the revised timeline, the extended Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) action date is May 12, 2027, giving the FDA additional time to review information provided in support of the NDA.

If no major deficiencies are identified during the ongoing review, the agency plans to communicate proposed labeling requests and any anticipated postmarketing requirement requests, if necessary, by April 12, 2027.

The shares were trading at $129.50, down 14.5% from the previous close.

data.title: Fed shouldn’t hike again after December – OnePoint BFG Wealth’s Peter Boockvar
data.description:
The Federal Reserve should not raise interest rates again after December, said Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer of OnePoint BFG Wealth Partners.

He cited turmoil in the AI tech trade, declining industrial metals prices, and falling crude oil prices .

"I just don't see how the Fed will hike again after December, if they even do then, if this selloff and AI CapEx concerns continue," he said.

The investment strategist pointed to the outsized role that artificial intelligence plays in the current economy as the reason for the Fed to exercise caution. Data center construction accounts for roughly half of GDP growth, AI-related companies represent approximately half of the S&P 500's (SP500) market capitalization, and the sector drives about 75% of earnings growth.

He noted that upper-income consumers are heavily dependent on the wealth effect from a stock market largely propelled by the AI trade.

"If the economic contribution from the data center build wasn't about half of GDP growth, if it wasn't about half the S&P 500 in terms of market cap, if it wasn't about 75% of earnings growth right now, and if the upper-income U.S. consumer wasn't so dependent on the wealth effect of a higher stock market mostly being driven by the AI trade, I'd say the Fed can look past this all with their inflation focus, but that's not where we stand," Boockvar explained.

While he expressed confidence that Kevin Warsh is monitoring these developments, he suggested some Fed colleagues "aren't reading the full room."

Peter Tchir, head of Macro Strategy at Academy Securities, echoed similar concerns about monetary policy tightening.

"They should probably avoid hiking in December too," he said, reinforcing the broader skepticism among market strategists about near-term rate increases.

data.title: How to Support Your Grandchildren Without Straining Your Finances — WSJ
data.description:
By Joann S. Lublin

Can you spoil your kids' kids without spoiling the Bank of Grandma and Grandpa? Maybe.

Older Americans are shelling out more dough than ever for their grandchildren. But problems sometimes arise when they express love too generously or unequally.

The average U.S. grandparent spends $3,917 a year on their offspring's progeny, representing outlays of $234 billion by about 60 million people, concludes a 2025 survey by Senior List, an online resource for older adults. The total is nearly five times as high as the estimated $52 billion that grandparents spent in 2009.

Today's grandparents often pitch in by subsidizing expensive needs such as private school, child care, housing, weddings, car purchases and vacations. Multigenerational trips, dubbed "gencations," have become especially popular.

But there are downsides. About 39% of those canvassed by Senior List feel obligated to ensure their grandchildren never go without — even if that strains their finances. Yet 62% of surveyed grandparents already have or would consider pulling money from retirement or savings accounts despite possibly endangering their future economic well-being.

In other cases, financial gifts for grandchildren cause tensions due to uneven treatment of grown offspring.

Here are strategies for managing your giving to grandchildren:

Establish boundaries

Set clear limits on gift amounts and their purposes that reflect your core values, experts suggest.

One possibility is setting up a "generosity account" — a nonreplenishable sum that you'll gradually disperse via your brokerage or savings account.

"The amount cannot in any way jeopardize your own financial security," says Stacy Francis, chief executive of Francis Financial, a New York advisory firm that says it coined the generosity term.

Francis cites a Florida client as a good example of staying financially secure. That retired therapist made enough money by selling her bigger New York home and downsizing to launch a $500,000 generosity account for her then 5-year-old grandson's educational and camp expenses. He's now 15, Francis continues, and "she has not added any additional money to this account."

Rachel Lawrence, head of advice and planning for personal-finance app Monarch Money, recommends that grandparents create an annual family-support fund within their written household budget. "Setting one number for a lifetime of grandkids' financial gifts is good in theory," she says. "But in practice, life changes."

Informal boundaries worked well for Jack Thomas, a semiretired real-estate developer in Cotuit, Mass. His four adult grandchildren grew up nearby.

After three learned to drive, he bought each a used vehicle — with strings. He says he insisted they pay for at least 10% of its purchase because "you're learning that life isn't an endless free ride."

His oldest grandson covered 10% of a pickup truck's $20,000 price tag. But Thomas also rejected that youth's subsequent request for a $12,000 motorboat by repeating a favorite so-called Papa-ism: "There are no limits on my love. But there are limitations on my money and spending."

Be transparent

Arrange candid, yearly chats with offspring so they understand your rationale for varied levels of aiding their children. If your intentions change, they can revise their own financial plans.

"You don't have to tell them what's in the portfolio down to the penny," says Stephanie Zepeda, a licensed marriage and family therapist in Houston. "Be as transparent as you can comfortably be."

A prepared script may make it easier to raise touchy issues such as your uneven support. Yet regular transparency about grandchild generosity doesn't always happen.

Nick Hager, a retired airline pilot in West Linn, Ore., embraced transparency belatedly. He and his wife set up "529" education-saving plans soon after their older son's 11-year-old boy and second son's 14-year-old girl were born.

However, Hager didn't remember that he never told his eldest about creating and funding the grandson's 529 account until asked about it for this article. "Our first conversation must have made me question my memory," the 82-year-old says.

His older son was pleasantly surprised to learn about the 529 plan and its sizable value, according to Hager. The plan was worth about $172,000 as of Nov. 13. "Future chats will take place as needed," Hager adds.

Have your adviser play bad cop

The best advisers — armed with their objective, holistic view of their clients' financial situations — serve neutrally as the bad cop. "They take the emotion right out of the room," says Pam Krueger, chief executive of Wealthramp, a matching platform for fee-only financial advisers. "They explain the why and how."

Having an adviser play that role proves especially useful when grown offspring don't recognize that your monetary largess toward grandchildren represents a pricey personal sacrifice.

Francis, the advisory firm CEO, assumed this role so an older New York client could rebuff her daughter's demand that she continue to significantly subsidize her grandson's private-school tuition and certain medical expenses. The long-divorced homemaker asked Francis to inform the daughter about risks to her own financial well-being from then gifting the youth $50,000 a year.

Summoning both women to her office, Francis explained how the mother "was going to run out of money soon if she kept on supporting her grandson to the same generous degree," the adviser recalls. "The daughter didn't realize that she was in any way putting her mom in a financially unsecure place."

In turn, Francis says, her client finally realized "that protecting her own financial security was not selfish."

These days, this woman bestows no more than $17,500 annually on her grandson. And Francis reviews additional major money requests from family members to facilitate their possible rejection.

Pay some bills directly

You must submit a federal gift-tax return if you give a grandchild more than $19,000 during a year. But you can avoid gift-tax limits and possible taxes by directly paying providers for qualified medical costs or educational expenses such as college tuition.

This tactic offers another advantage. "Paying college tuition directly allows you to keep control of your money for as long as you want," says Quentara Costa, a certified financial planner and founder of Powwow, a financial-advisory firm in North Andover, Mass.

Some individuals fear funding their newborn grandchild's 529 plan for 18 years will make it difficult to handle their own hefty costs late in life, such as long-term care, according to Costa. "It can feel a little scary." she says.

One possible solution: Combine your grandchild's modest 529 account with direct-tuition payments. Thanks to those plans' flexibility, you can transfer unused money to another blood relative.

For example, Costa completed two college degrees assisted by a 529 plan that her grandmother had established, another relative's direct-tuition gift and a scholarship. She says the account still held almost $25,000 upon her 2008 graduation, even after withdrawing more than $33,000 for her degrees.

Costa's now 11-year-old daughter became the plan's beneficiary in 2024. Today, the girl's 529 plan is worth about $368,000.

data.title: BayCom Corp Announces Appointment of New Director
data.description:
BayCom Corp () (the “Company”), the holding company for United Business Bank (the “Bank”), today announced that Stanley R. Ivie was appointed as a director of the Company and as a director of the Bank, effective November 17, 2026.

Mr. Ivie brings decades of leadership, risk management, and regulatory experience in the banking industry and currently serves as Chairman of the California Bankers Association. Most recently, he served Banc of California and its holding company, Banc of California, Inc., as Executive Vice President and Head of Government and Regulatory Affairs from November 2023 until he retired in February 2026. He led Banc of California’s regulatory strategy, served as its liaison to legislative and regulatory agencies and oversaw its Community Reinvestment Act, corporate sustainability and strategic planning programs. Mr. Ivie served as Executive Vice President and Chief Risk Officer of Pacific Western Bank and PacWest Bancorp from March 2016 until PacWest’s merger with Banc of California in November 2023. In his role there, he oversaw Pacific Western Bank’s enterprise risk management strategy and the policies and practices that assess and mitigate financial, operational and strategic risks, including those related to cybersecurity, fraud, modeling and the Bank Secrecy Act.

Previously, Mr. Ivie held various leadership positions with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), including Regional Director for the FDIC’s San Francisco and Dallas regions. Before joining the FDIC's Supervision Division in 2005, he served as the Deputy Director for the Division of Resolutions and Receiverships in Dallas, where he oversaw the resolution of failing banks nationwide.

“I'm thrilled to welcome Stan to our Board. He is one of the most accomplished risk and regulatory leaders in the industry, and very few people bring his depth of experience. We expect that Stan will play a big role in helping us build this business the right way in the years ahead,” said Bill Black, Executive Vice Chairman.

“We are delighted to welcome Stan Ivie to our Board. Stan brings a rare combination of perspectives,” said Christopher Baron, Chief Executive Officer. “He spent more than three decades at the FDIC and then managed risk and government and regulatory affairs from inside commercial banks larger than ours. His judgment and experience will be invaluable as we continue to grow.”

“Stan Ivie is an excellent addition to BayCom,” said Lloyd Kendall, Chairman of the Board. “His regulatory experience and knowledge, strategic risk management, and leadership will be invaluable to the Board as we continue to execute our strategy.”

About BayCom Corp

The Company, through its wholly owned operating subsidiary, United Business Bank, offers a full range of loans, including SBA, CalCAP, FSA and USDA guaranteed loans, and deposit products and services to businesses and their affiliates in California, Washington, New Mexico and Colorado. The Bank is an Equal Housing Lender and a member of FDIC. The Company’s common stock is traded on the NASDAQ under the symbol “BCML”. For more information, go to www.unitedbusinessbank.com.

Forward-Looking Statements

This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including statements regarding the Company's strategic plans and expected benefits thereof. Forward-looking statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. These risks include, without limitation, the Company's ability to successfully execute its management transition, retain key employees and clients, and achieve its strategic objectives. data.title: Quebecor Pitches Telus Bid As Survival Tactic Amid Musk, Bezos Wireless Ambitions — Analysis
data.description:
(17:54 GMT) *Quebecor Bid for Telus Meant to Deal With Satellite-to-Phone Threat
(17:54 GMT) *Quebecor: Space Companies Could Pose Threat to Canadian Telecoms
(17:54 GMT) *Quebecor CEO Peladeau: Warned Canadian Officials About Satellite-to-Phone Disruption
(17:54 GMT) Quebecor Pitches Telus Bid As Survival Tactic Amid Musk, Bezos Wireless Ambitions — Analysis

By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA-Quebecor Chief Executive Pierre-Karl Peladeau launched his bold $22 billion bid to take over telecom rival Telus with Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos in mind.

Part of Peladeau's pitch to Canadian authorities, which would need to greenlight a merger of the No. 3 and 4 wireless providers by subscribers, is the need for a domestic telecommunications company with the infrastructure and financial wherewithal to thrive in the next frontier of wireless competition: space. Case in point, he said, is Musk's $8 billion deal last month, through SpaceX, to acquire cellular spectrum licenses. The Federal Communications Commission also has approved SpaceX's bid to launch up to 15,000 satellites dedicated to mobile service.

Amazon.com's space unit, Leo, also has filed with the FCC for approval to launch more than 5,000 satellites to deliver direct-to-phone service.

"For telecom companies in Canada, to make sure that they will remain competitive, we need to think longer than six months or even three years, [because] telecom will be also integrating and introducing nonterrestrial networks," Peladeau said in an interview earlier this week. "This is of importance for telecom companies, and this is of importance for political authorities."

A Quebecor spokesman later said the CEO remarks were focused on foreign efforts from the likes of Musk's SpaceX and Bezos's Leo, which if replicated in Canada poses "a credible threat to the continued existence of a Canadian-owned company in our country."

Peladeau has a point, said Erik Bohlin, an expert in telecommunications policy at Western University's Ivey Business School in London, Ontario. "There is quite a bit of nervousness in the industry," he said.

Policymakers in Canada, Europe and elsewhere are aware of the pending disruption to the wireless market posed by satellites, Bohlin said, adding officials will face pressure to allow entry to SpaceX and other space firms into their markets should the result be lower cellphone costs. "This is urgent for Canada to think about," he added.

Peladeau said he's set to meet Telus next week on next steps to reach a finalized deal. Telus said the Quebecor proposal is subject to heightened regulatory risk, as a transaction would require approval from the antitrust watchdog and telecommunications regulator. According to Quebecor, a merger with Telus would produce the biggest wireless provider in Canada with 15 million subscribers - 4.5 million from Quebecor and 10.4 million from Telus. Rogers Communications has more than 12 million, and BCE's Bell Canada unit about 10.4 million as well.

Research from Accenture unit Ookla indicates SpaceX, through Starlink, holds about 5% of Canada's broadband-internet service market, reflecting rural and remote customers. SpaceX also has a deal with Rogers Communications to help expand Rogers's ability to bring satellite-to-phone coverage in Canada. Rogers CEO Tony Staffieri told analysts during a third-quarter conference call that the company is looking to deepen ties with SpaceX.

A representative from SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said this week the emergence of satellite technology has the potential to further drive down wireless prices, and officials are preparing an update to telecom policy to reflect potential new technology. In theory, he said, fewer players in the wireless market can still produce lower prices, "and we need to take informed decisions on that."

Mark Warner, a Toronto-based trade and competition lawyer with U.S. and Canadian clients, said the best way Peladeau's bid can fly with regulators is if Quebecor is successful in arguing that "the relevant market is not wireless and internet, but it's wireless, internet and satellite."

data.title: Bitcoin Nears One-Year Low as Tech Selloff Intensifies — 2nd Update
data.description:
By Dean Seal and Joe Stonor

Major cryptocurrencies fell Friday, with bitcoin tumbling close to its lowest level this year as the tech-led selloff in global markets intensifies.

Bitcoin was down 6.5%, at $58,928, extending a string of losses in the past week into a 30% loss over the past month. The last time it traded this low was for a single day at the end of June, according to Coinglass data. The last time before that in 2024.

Ether was down 8.7%, at $1,622, sitting close to its own 2026 low.

The tumult comes after a tough Thursday session when Anthropic's initial public offering failed to spark a broader market rally. Some of Anthropic's debut gains were funded with capital investors cycling out of stocks and crypto assets.

Instead of leading a tech stock recovery on Friday, Anthropic was swallowed up in another selloff. The Nasdaq composite is down 3.6%, while Anthropic shares are down 13%, close to their IPO price.

Heading into the Friday session, the entire crypto market was already dealing with a 2% drop in its total capitalization, to $2.11 trillion, according to FxPro analyst Alex Kuptsikevich. That marked a return to mid-summer lows, where it bottomed out at $2.06 trillion.

Increased institutional adoption of digital assets is proving a near-term headwind for crypto assets, rather than a boon, Nidal Abdel Hadi, chief executive of investment group Finoro, said. Higher correlation to stocks makes crypto more vulnerable to broader risk-off sentiment shifts.

"The provocative possibility is that bitcoin's integration into mainstream finance has weakened its ability to behave independently of traditional liquidity cycles," Hadi said.

data.title: Congress struggles to avert US shutdown as Iran war divides lawmakers
data.description:
Key points:
  • Current federal funding expires after December 11, leaving Congress three weeks to reach a deal
  • Senate bipartisan funding package would need 60 votes to pass in 100-seat chamber
  • Democrats split on tying agency funding to limits on Trump's military action against Iran

By David Morgan

Congress could be headed for a pre-Christmas government shutdown as divisions over the Iran war and President Donald Trump's demand for $350 billion in new Pentagon spending threaten to derail any funding deal, lawmakers from both parties warned.

Lawmakers have only three weeks to iron out an agreement to keep federal agencies operating after December 11, when current funding is set to expire. But the two parties remained far apart as they prepared for a one-week Thanksgiving holiday break, especially in the 100-seat Senate, where a bipartisan funding package would need 60 votes to pass.

Republicans and Democrats aim to find common ground on a stopgap measure to fund government operations into early next year, when Democrats take control of the Senate and House of Representatives after a sweeping victory in the November midterms. They also hold out hope of passing some full-year appropriations bills in the current lame-duck session to fund parts of the government through the current fiscal year, which ends on September 30.

But each party faces its own dilemma over how to move forward. Republicans are hesitant to pursue the partisan path Trump has demanded on defense funding, citing differences over what should be included in such a bill. Democrats are divided over whether limiting funding for the president's Iran war is worth a government shutdown.

'WE DON'T WANT TO FUND THE WAR'

Republicans have largely sought to paint Democrats as willing to trigger the fourth partial government shutdown of Trump's second term, claiming Democrats have not been willing to negotiate a funding package before a December 1 party leadership election between current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and challenger Chris Van Hollen.

But some signs of progress had begun to emerge by the end of the week.

"The American people don't need another government shutdown," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Tuesday. "I think that would be a colossal mistake and a real disservice to the people of this country." On Friday, he told reporters that "some good conversations" were taking place on funding but there were "no deals yet."

Senate Democrats acknowledged they are wrestling with the question of whether to insist on language to restrict Trump's use of force against Iran, a prospect most Republicans reject, even if it means cutting off funds to federal agencies and workers ahead of the Christmas holiday.

"The big obstacle is that we don't want to fund the war, we don't want to shut down, how do you solve that," said Senator Peter Welch, a Vermont Democrat. "That's the Gordian knot."

Democrats have already forced three shutdowns since Trump returned to power in January 2025, including the longest large-scale shutdown in US history. Earlier this year, they cut off Homeland Security funding after federal immigration agents fatally shot two US citizens in Minneapolis.

Senator John Hickenlooper, a Colorado Democrat, declined to state his own position on funding but suggested the pain American families are now suffering from high energy prices due to the Iran war could justify another cutoff of funding.

"A shutdown of government right before the holidays is a tough nut. You wouldn't do it if it wasn't dire. This is pretty dire. The war's gone on for a long time, and I think we saw in the election that it's very unpopular," Hickenlooper told reporters.

Some Democrats adamantly oppose a shutdown.

"Shutting the government down doesn't stop the war," said Representative Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. "Everybody feels very strongly. They want to end this war ... How do you strategically move to get that done? Without shutting down the government - that's where I am on this issue."

'WE'RE GOING TO RUN OUT OF TIME'

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins told reporters that Democrats were not seeking language on Iran in exchange for agreement on a bipartisan short-term government funding package known as a continuing resolution, or CR, but in relation to new defense funding sought by Trump.

Senate Republicans have failed to agree on whether to meet Trump's $350 billion defense funding request through a partisan maneuver called budget reconciliation, which would allow them to circumvent Democratic opposition and enact such legislation with a simple majority vote.

The Senate Republican conference discussed Trump's request for a partisan defense bill behind closed doors for more than an hour this week and decided instead to pursue bipartisan talks with Democrats on a $1.1 trillion defense appropriations bill proposed by Republicans that contains only $69 billion of Trump's funding request.

Republicans say a partisan bill remains on the table, which could complicate a bipartisan deal.

"We're going to run out of time if we don't expedite either more communications with both sides of the aisle, or if we can't come to a consensus on exactly what it is would be in a reconciliation product," Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Reuters.

Republicans and Democrats both held out the possibility of passing at least some of the 12 full-year appropriations bills needed to fully fund federal agencies for the remainder of fiscal 2027 and funding the remainder of government agencies through a CR.

"Being able to finish all 12 bills is not possible. But I believe we can get out a number of them ... and then deal with where we need to be on the CR," DeLauro said.
